facts.statement: The scientific name of the genus is Taurovenator.
facts.quote: taxon: Taurovenator

facts.statement: Taurovenator was named by Motta and colleagues in 2016.
facts.quote: authority: Motta et al., 2016

facts.statement: The type species of the genus is Taurovenator violantei.
facts.quote: type_species: Taurovenator violantei

facts.statement: Taurovenator was initially known only from a single postorbital bone found in the Huincul Formation.
facts.quote: Initially only known from a single postorbital skull bone described from the Huincul Formation

facts.statement: The holotype fossil, a right postorbital, was unearthed by Matias Motta in 2005 from the lower member of the Huincul Formation.
facts.quote: In 2005, a right postorbital of a theropod dinosaur was unearthed by Argentine paleontologist Matias Motta from a section of sandstone strata deriving from the lower member of the Huincul Formation

facts.statement: The fossil was found on Violante Farm in Rio Negro Province, Argentina.
facts.quote: The strata located on the Violante Farm, a farm located in Rio Negro Province, Argentina

facts.statement: The postorbital was formally described as the holotype of Taurovenator violantei in 2016.
facts.quote: This postorbital remained undescribed until in 2016, when Matias Motta and colleagues described the postorbital as the holotype (name-bearing specimen) of a new genus and species of carcharodontosaurid dinosaur, Taurovenator violantei

facts.statement: The specific name violantei honors the Violante Farm where the fossil was found.
facts.quote: the specific name is in honor of Violante Farm where the postorbital was unearthed

facts.statement: Some paleontologists have debated whether Taurovenator is synonymous with the genus Mapusaurus.
facts.quote: Debate came about over the validity of the species, with some paleontologists arguing that Taurovenator was synonymous with the earlier-named carcharodontosaurid Mapusaurus

facts.statement: Coria et al. (2019) suggested Taurovenator is synonymous with Mapusaurus because their original distinguishing features were shared.
facts.quote: Coria et al. (2019) suggesting that Taurovenator is synonymous with Mapusaurus, considering both of its original autapomorphies as shared with Mapusaurus

facts.statement: Researcher Mickey Mortimer believed Taurovenator was synonymous with Mapusaurus due to insufficient diagnostic material.
facts.quote: Researcher Mickey Mortimer also believed that Taurovenator was synonymous with Mapusaurus due to the lack of sufficient material and diagnostic traits for the genus

facts.statement: A previously undescribed partial skeleton found at the same site was referred to Taurovenator in 2024.
facts.quote: In 2024, this specimen was described and, despite not overlapping in material with the holotype, was referred to Taurovenator

facts.statement: Differences in stratigraphic layers suggest Taurovenator, Meraxes, and Mapusaurus may not have lived at the same time, supporting Taurovenator's validity.
facts.quote: It is for these reasons that the three carcharodontosaurids found at Huincul were potentially not coeval, supporting the argument for Taurovenator's validity

facts.statement: Taurovenator is classified as a very large carcharodontosaurid.
facts.quote: Taurovenator is a very large carcharodontosaurid

facts.statement: Taurovenator is among the largest known theropod dinosaurs and one of the biggest terrestrial carnivores.
facts.quote: This puts Taurovenator among the largest theropod dinosaurs known and therefore one of the biggest terrestrial carnivores known to science

facts.statement: The skull of Taurovenator was estimated to be around 135 cm long based on comparisons with related species.
facts.quote: The maximum length of the skull of MPCA-Pv 803 was estimated to be around 135 cm based on the more complete skulls of relatives like Meraxes.

facts.statement: Taurovenator possessed a postorbital bone that projected outward like a horn, a trait distinct from other carcharodontosaurids.
facts.quote: The postorbital is strongly rugose and projected out like a horn, markedly different from the orbital bosses of other carcharodontosaurids.

facts.statement: The horn-like projection on Taurovenator's postorbital measured 3-4 cm in height and 2-3 cm in diameter.
facts.quote: The projection measuring 3-4 cm in height and 2-3 cm in diameter.

facts.statement: Two preserved teeth of Taurovenator were each approximately 4 cm in length.
facts.quote: Two teeth are preserved from Taurovenator, both of which are large, around 4 cm in length.

facts.statement: Taurovenator's teeth featured well-developed blood grooves and notably deep enamel wrinkles, characteristic of carcharodontosaurids.
facts.quote: Their blood grooves are well developed and their enamel wrinkles are notably deep, a distinct characteristic of carcharodontosaurid teeth.

facts.statement: Taurovenator's neck vertebrae had prominent neural spines with flange-like dorsal tips.
facts.quote: Distinctively, Taurovenators neck vertebrae bore prominent neural spines with flange-like dorsal tips.

facts.statement: Researchers described the interlocking neck vertebrae of Taurovenator as a unique "cervical complex" resembling overlapping roof tiles.
facts.quote: The authors describing this morphology termed this unusual structure a "cervical complex", and likened them to overlapping roof tiles.

facts.statement: One of the known dorsal vertebrae of Taurovenator consisted of a neural arch that was 52 cm high.
facts.quote: One is composed of a centrum, but the other is composed of a very tall, 52 cm high neural arch.

facts.statement: Taurovenator had some of the smallest arms among known allosauroids, measuring 65-68% of the femur length.
facts.quote: Taurovenator had proportionately some of the smallest arms of all known allosauroids, being 65-68% of the length of the femur.

facts.statement: Taurovenator shared with Meraxes an enlarged claw on the second toe that was approximately 20% longer than the third toe's equivalent phalanx.
facts.quote: Taurovenator also shares with Meraxes an enlarged ungual claw on the second toe, approximately 20% longer than the equivalent phalanx of the third toe and more laterally compressed.

facts.statement: Taurovenator fossils were found in the Huincul Formation, which consists of yellowish and greenish fine-to-medium grain sandstones, some containing volcanic ash.
facts.quote: The Huincul Formation is composed of yellowish and greenish sandstones of fine-to-medium grain, some of which are tuffaceous.

facts.statement: The age of Taurovenator's deposits was previously estimated to be between the Cenomanian and Turonian, or possibly the Early Turonian to Late Santonian.
facts.quote: Earlier findings suggested a Cenomanian–Turonian age, or possibly an Early Turonian to Late Santonian age.

facts.statement: The environment where Taurovenator lived was a braided river drainage system.
facts.quote: The deposits represent the drainage system of a braided river.

facts.statement: Fossilized pollen from the Huincul Formation indicates a diverse plant community including ferns, gymnosperms, and angiosperms.
facts.quote: Fossilised pollen indicates a wide variety of plants were present in the Huincul Formation.

facts.statement: Motta et al. (2016) classified Taurovenator as a derived member of Carcharodontosauridae, closely related to Giganotosaurus, Carcharodontosaurus, and Mapusaurus.
facts.quote: Classification Motta et al. (2016) suggested that Taurovenator occupied a derived position within Carcharodontosauridae, comparing it to Giganotosaurus, Carcharodontosaurus and Mapusaurus in particular.

facts.statement: Coria et al. (2019) debated that Taurovenator is synonymous with Mapusaurus, arguing that its unique features were shared with Mapusaurus.
facts.quote: Coria et al. (2019) suggested that Taurovenator is synonymous with Mapusaurus, considering both of its original autapomorphies as shared with Mapusaurus and also pointing out that both taxa shared a curved lateral margin of the palpebral.

facts.statement: A 2025 study by Cau and Paterna debated the classification of Taurovenator, placing it outside the family Carcharodontosauridae.
facts.quote: In 2025, Cau and Paterna recovered Taurovenator as an allosauroid outside Carcharodontosauridae.

facts.statement: Taurovenator fossils were found at Rancho Violante on the shores of Lake Ezequiel Ramos Mexía in Río Negro Province, Patagonia, Argentina.
facts.quote: Sus restos se encontraron en el Rancho Violante, en las orillas del lago Ezequiel Ramos Mexía en la provincia de Río Negro, Patagonia Argentina

facts.statement: The holotype of Taurovenator violantei, specimen MPCA PV 802, was found in the Huincul Formation dating from the Cenomanian to Turonian stages.
facts.quote: Allí se encontró el holotipo de Taurovenator violantei, MPCA PV 802 se encuentra en una capa de la Formación Huincul que data del Cenomaniense al Turoniense

facts.statement: The Taurovenator holotype is housed in the vertebrate paleontology collection of the "Carlos Ameghino" Provincial Museum.
facts.quote: El fósil es parte de la colección de paleontología de vertebrados del Museo Provincial "Carlos Ameghino".

facts.statement: Taurovenator violantei was named and described in 2016 by Matías J. Motta, Alexis M. Aranciaga Rolando, Sebastián Rozadilla, Federico E. Agnolin, Nicolás R. Chimento, Federico Brisson Egli, and Emilio Fernando Novas.
facts.quote: En 2016, la especie tipo Taurovenator violantei fue nombrada y descrita por Matías J. Motta, Alexis M. Aranciaga Rolando, Sebastián Rozadilla Federico E. Agnolin Nicolás R. Chimento, Federico Brisson Egli y Emilio Fernando Novas.

facts.statement: The genus name Taurovenator combines the Latin words for 'bull' and 'hunter', referring to a distinctive horn behind the eye socket.
facts.quote: El nombre del género es una combinación del latín taurus, "toro" y venator, "cazador", y se refiere a un cuerno distintivo detrás de la cuenca del ojo.

facts.statement: The species name violantei honors the owner of the ranch, Enzo Violante.
facts.quote: El nombre de la especie hace honor al dueño del rancho, Enzo Violante.

facts.statement: Taurovenator lived in the middle Cretaceous, approximately 96 to 91 million years ago (Cenomanian to Turonian), in what is now South America.
facts.quote: Taurovenator violantei es la única especie conocida del género extinto Taurovenator, un dinosaurio terópodo carcarodontosáurido que vivió a mediados del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente entre 96 a 91 millones de años, desde el Cenomaniense a Turoniense, en lo que es hoy Sudamérica.

facts.statement: Taurovenator is classified in the family Carcharodontosauridae.
facts.quote: familia: Carcharodontosauridae

facts.statement: The genus Taurovenator was established by Motta et al. in 2016.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Motta et al., 2016

facts.statement: Taurovenator is considered a medium-sized theropod, based on an orbital section length of 12 centimeters.
facts.quote: Gracias a la longitud de la sección de la órbita, de 12 centímetros, se puede ver que Taurovenator es un terópodo de tamaño mediano.

facts.statement: The orbital horn is relatively robust but small and rounded, and clearly disconnected from the edge.
facts.quote: El cuerno de la región orbital es relativamente robusto pero diminuto y redondeado y claramente desconectado del borde.

facts.statement: The outer wall of the descending ramus is very porous, indicating it may belong to an older individual.
facts.quote: La pared exterior de la rama es muy porosa, una señal de que es posible poner un viejo individuo.

facts.statement: It has been suggested that Taurovenator is a synonym of Mapusaurus.
facts.quote: Se ha sugerido que Taurovenator es sinónimo de Mapusaurus.

facts.statement: The parent group for Taurovenator is Carcharodontosauridae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Carcharodontosauridae

facts.statement: The Paleobi Database records the time range of Taurovenator as the Albian, between 110.1 and 106.3 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Albian to Albian (110.1 to 106.3 million years ago)
